gaps.concept: Breast density and alcohol use independently increase breast cancer risk.
gaps.why_tested: A risk-factor stem asks about exposures beyond reproductive history and inherited mutations.

gaps.concept: Nonproliferative breast changes confer little added risk; proliferative lesions without atypia confer modest risk; atypical hyperplasia confers substantially greater risk.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy stem asks how a benign finding changes future cancer risk.

gaps.concept: Atypical ductal hyperplasia resembles low-grade DCIS but involves only part of a duct or a limited area.
gaps.why_tested: A histology stem asks the student to distinguish a precursor lesion from DCIS.

gaps.concept: Inherited BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants act as autosomal dominant cancer predispositions; tumor formation typically requires somatic loss of the remaining functional allele.
gaps.why_tested: A pedigree and tumor-genetics stem tests the two-hit mechanism.

gaps.concept: BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants also increase ovarian cancer risk.
gaps.why_tested: A family history combining breast and ovarian cancers points to hereditary BRCA susceptibility.

gaps.concept: Normal breast ducts and lobules have a myoepithelial layer and basement membrane; loss of these boundaries supports invasion.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy stem asks the student to distinguish in situ from invasive carcinoma.

gaps.concept: DCIS is usually unilateral and can progress to invasive carcinoma in the affected breast.
gaps.why_tested: A stem contrasts the natural history of DCIS with LCIS-associated bilateral risk.

gaps.concept: LCIS consists of discohesive, relatively uniform cells expanding lobules and usually lacks mammographic calcifications.
gaps.why_tested: An incidental biopsy finding must be distinguished from calcification-associated DCIS.

gaps.concept: High-grade DCIS commonly shows HER2 positivity; classic LCIS is usually ER positive and HER2 negative.
gaps.why_tested: A biomarker or histology stem asks the student to identify an in situ lesion.

gaps.concept: Invasive breast carcinoma commonly presents as a painless, hard, irregular mass; fibrosis pulling Cooper ligaments causes skin dimpling or nipple retraction.
gaps.why_tested: A physical-examination stem asks for the mechanism of a characteristic malignant finding.

gaps.concept: Invasive lobular carcinoma can infiltrate diffusely without a distinct mass and may contain signet-ring cells.
gaps.why_tested: A subtle imaging finding or signet-ring histology stem points to lobular carcinoma.

gaps.concept: Invasive lobular carcinoma has a relative tendency to metastasize to the peritoneum, gastrointestinal tract, and ovaries.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with prior lobular carcinoma develops an unusual abdominal metastatic lesion.

gaps.concept: Medullary carcinoma can have a better prognosis than its high-grade appearance suggests.
gaps.why_tested: A morphology-and-prognosis stem tests the medullary subtype's characteristic exception.

gaps.concept: Mucinous carcinoma shows tumor cells floating in abundant extracellular mucin.
gaps.why_tested: A histology image asks the student to identify the subtype.

gaps.concept: Tubular carcinoma forms small, well-differentiated, angulated tubules infiltrating stroma.
gaps.why_tested: A histology image asks the student to distinguish a favorable invasive subtype.

gaps.concept: Metaplastic carcinoma may show malignant squamous or spindle-cell differentiation.
gaps.why_tested: A breast tumor with non-glandular malignant cells must be classified.

gaps.concept: Male breasts generally lack developed lobules, making lobular carcinoma exceptionally rare in men.
gaps.why_tested: A male breast cancer stem asks why ductal histology predominates.

gaps.concept: Nottingham histologic grade scores tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic activity.
gaps.why_tested: A pathology report asks which microscopic features determine tumor grade.

gaps.concept: ER and PR positivity predicts benefit from endocrine therapy.
gaps.why_tested: A receptor-profile stem asks which treatment class is likely to work.

gaps.concept: Triple-negative tumors lack ER, PR, and HER2 targets, so endocrine and HER2-directed therapies are ineffective.
gaps.why_tested: A receptor-profile stem asks why those targeted treatments are unsuitable.

gaps.concept: HER2 dimerization activates PI3K–AKT and RAS–MAPK growth signaling; pertuzumab blocks HER2 dimerization.
gaps.why_tested: A molecular-mechanism stem asks how HER2 amplification drives growth or how pertuzumab acts.

gaps.concept: HER2 protein overexpression is assessed by immunohistochemistry; ERBB2 gene amplification can be confirmed by in situ hybridization.
gaps.why_tested: A pathology stem asks how an equivocal HER2 result is resolved.

gaps.concept: Tamoxifen antagonizes estrogen receptors in breast tissue but has estrogen-like effects in endometrium and bone.
gaps.why_tested: A drug-mechanism stem asks why tamoxifen treats breast cancer yet increases endometrial risk.

gaps.concept: Aromatase inhibitors reduce peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen; ovarian estrogen production limits their use alone before menopause.
gaps.why_tested: A premenopausal versus postmenopausal treatment stem tests the source of estrogen.

gaps.concept: CDK4/6 inhibitors prevent retinoblastoma-protein phosphorylation and G1-to-S cell-cycle progression.
gaps.why_tested: A drug-mechanism stem asks how these agents slow hormone-receptor-positive tumor growth.

gaps.concept: PARP inhibition is synthetically lethal in BRCA-deficient tumors because unrepaired DNA breaks accumulate.
gaps.why_tested: A BRCA-mutant tumor stem asks why a DNA-repair inhibitor is effective.

gaps.concept: Breast cancer bone metastases are commonly osteolytic and may cause hypercalcemia.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with breast cancer develops bone pain, lytic lesions, and elevated calcium.
